title: Mansa Musa and the Empires of West Africa

cards.h: The pilgrim who crashed Cairo's gold market
cards.b:
In 1324, a king from West Africa arrived in Cairo on the way to Mecca. He came with a huge caravan and so much gold that he gave and spent it freely.

An Arab writer, al-Umari, said the price of gold in Cairo stayed low for about twelve years. His name was Mansa Musa.

Mali was founded around 1235 by Sundiata Keita, who defeated a rival king at the battle of Kirina. His story is told in the oral epic of the griots.

Mali sat on the Niger river, between the forest where gold was mined and the Sahara desert where salt came from.
Caravans of camels crossed the Sahara. The Mali rulers taxed the trade. Timbuktu and Gao became rich towns.

Musa ruled from about 1312 to 1337. His pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 is the stuff of legend. Accounts speak of tens of thousands of people and many camels carrying gold. Numbers are probably exaggerated, but the display clearly shocked Cairo.

On the way home he brought back scholars and an architect. In Timbuktu a great mosque, Djinguereber, and later Sankore became centres of learning.

A Spanish map of 1375, the Catalan Atlas, shows a king on a throne holding a golden nugget, labelled as the ruler of Mali. It put West Africa on Europe's mind.

Ibn Battuta, the great traveller, visited Mali in 1352-53, in the reign of Musa's brother Sulayman.

Mali weakened in the 1400s. The Songhai Empire under Sunni Ali and then Askia Muhammad took over, with Gao as capital. Timbuktu's libraries kept thousands of manuscripts.

Songhai fell to a Moroccan invasion in 1591.

cards.h: Was Musa the richest man ever?
cards.b:
Myth: he was worth hundreds of billions of dollars.Fact: there are no records to calculate this. Medieval wealth cannot be compared with today's. What we can say: he was famously generous and Mali was extremely rich in gold.

Also, Musa did not 'found' Timbuktu; it was already a town. Another caution: our main sources are Arabic writers, who may exaggerate.

Two travellers' worlds

Mansa Musa left Mali for his pilgrimage in 1324. In Delhi, Muhammad bin Tughluq took the throne in 1325. Two Muslim rulers, one on the Niger and one on the Yamuna, were among the richest in the world.

Both attempted bold experiments. Tughluq moved his capital to Daulatabad in 1327 and issued token currency around 1329. Musa's gold, spent in Cairo, caused prices there to fall for years.

A single traveller linked the two worlds. Ibn Battuta served as qadi of Delhi for years under Tughluq, then in 1352-53 visited Mali. No other writer saw both.

Five things to remember

  1. Mali was founded by Sundiata around 1235.
  2. Gold and salt drove the trade.
  3. Musa's Hajj in 1324 became famous.
  4. Timbuktu became a scholarly city.
  5. Songhai followed Mali.

Think about it

  • Why did gold in Cairo 'lose value'?
  • What makes a source reliable when it comes from outsiders?
